en: Such arrogance as this
He had never seen upon the earth.)
'My quarry has gone in; drive it out!
Flush my pheasant out for me!
Bring me my falcon!'
Though he said this many times, there was no reply.
At the orphan who was speaking
He would not even look.
Semetey burned again.
Your orphan of surpassing courage
Could not keep still in his fury,
'No post to tether a horse,
You are not alive, you have no soul,
Not a single hair upon your head,
No concern but charcoal!
I thought you human, but you have no dignity.
Are you a hero, Sary Taz?
I greet you, but there is no answer.
Are you an infidel, Sary Taz?
The road to Judgment is grievously hard.
I greet you, but there is no answer.
The man who keeps silent—
Seven generations of his fathers are infidels.
Blackened with soot from quenching charcoal,
A poor man master of a great forest,
He has no wealth but charcoal,
No life but his fire-steel.
The poor man shoves charcoal like a camel,
Master of Kul-Tokoy.
He grew up in the wilderness, seeing no human;
That foolish bald man, seeing no person,
Grew up in the dark forest, a grave.
The person who greets you—
Do you not see him, Sary Taz?
When your appointed end comes one day,
Will you not die, Sary Taz?
Will you take my falcon
And give it into my hand, Sary Taz?
Rather than make your living so,
Rather than stay alive like this,
Drink the fat of your fish,
Sary Taz, drink your mother's blood!
Sary Taz, I shall slaughter you.
If you greatly anger me,
I shall leave your forest deserted!
Even if you have eighty lives,
I shall slaughter you this moment,
I shall put you to death!'
Semetey pushed his horse forward.
When he came close,
Sary Taz stood and said:
'Damn your father's grave, orphan slave!
Waving your limbs as though full-grown,
As though you have only now become a man,
To Temir Khan's city,
Leaving your ocean in Talas,
What of you, orphan slave, living as a wanderer?
My own kin have become my enemies:
What of me, quenching charcoal?
You have reached twelve years of age,
And to this poor charcoal-burner's
Charcoal ground you come.
Damned orphan slave,
Your homeland is Kyrgyz Talas:
When will you go to your homeland?
The winning face of a little blue knucklebone,
Ysmayyl's hired falconer,
The townspeople's lucky cast,
Temir Khan's falconer!
Quenching charcoal in the wilds,
To my charcoal ground you come.
If you are a fierce hero, orphan,
You damned orphan slave,
When will you go to your people?'
In anger, Sary Taz
With his dark bowl, big as a cow's head,
From the bubbling dark spring
Scooped water once again.
With a 'Gurgle!' he took a mouthful,
With a 'Puff!' toward the charcoal
He turned and sprayed it.
Charcoal dust made it dark as night.
Surpassing his father, fierce Manas,
Semetey, his son,
Burned within, filled with rage.
Unable to keep still, the dear khan,
His dear life would not fit within a fist.
That bald man had spoken,
And his words had struck him hard,
Calling him a hired servant.
He burned and blazed like an ember,
His two eyes turned to fire.
Flames hissed from his mouth;
The frenzied orphan could not keep still.
From the bald man's words
He could not turn his neck away.
The heavy whip with dark handle
He grasped and swung round.
His head bent toward the fire,
Sary Taz's backside
Rose like a millstone.
The fleshy muscles of his fat rump
Looked extraordinary,
Standing out so plainly.
He could not draw back his outstretched arm,
Could not return without striking the bald man.
The heavy whip with dark handle
He grasped and swung round.
Upon the firm flesh of that fat rump,
The young lord, the mad slave,
Stepped close and brought it down.
When he struck, Sary Taz's
Voice was heard by God,
His head plunged into the charcoal.
His rather tight leather trousers
Burst where the blow fell.
Dark blood streamed like an irrigation ditch;
Before he drew back the whip,
It gushed along with it.
The bald man's sight grew dim.
Flesh from his rump, big as a large bowl,
Trailed out with the blow.
My bald man fled, scurrying,
'If he strikes again, I am done for!'
Taking refuge in his charcoal.
Scurrying along,
Ready to fling words of trouble,
Blood streamed down his shins.
Unable to walk, he stopped, swaying,
Speaking crooked, quarrelsome words,
Straddling like a lice-ridden horse.
His wing bent back,
He spoke defiant words.
Sary Taz, with his bowl-like eye,
Deprived of flesh from his rump,
Clutched his wound tightly.
Every bone in him ached.
Turning back, your elder Sary
Now cursed Semetey:
'Damned orphan slave!
You have no caravan descending from the slope.
For you to beat me bloody,
Your forty Kyrgyz forefathers have no vengeance here!
No one among the people wanders as you do.
For you to slash my backside open,
Your seven forefathers have no vengeance upon me!
This Kul-Tokoy is no Chinese land.
Your father, fierce Manas,
Had his lungs pierced and was killed—
You damned orphan slave,
I am not the Chinese Kongurbay!
Gird your waist firmly.
Kongurbay in Beijing
Slaughtered your valiant father:
Demand his blood-price from him!
This forest is no land of Beijing.
Your father's sworn brother Almambet
Was ambushed and shot—
I am not the Chinese Kozhozhash!
Gather your Kyrgyz caravan in Talas,
You staggering orphan slave!
Those who slaughtered your champions,
The Chinese people in Beijing—
Go and take your vengeance upon them!
Strike your ox's saddle sore!
Alas, alas, my fat rump!
Strike the liver of your dead father, Khan Manas!
You have grown strong: raid the Kyrgyz frontier!
Strike the gall of your mother Kanykei!
Strike all your forefathers!
Rather than strike my rump,
Boy, strike your mother's head!
My wing has been bent back.
Alas upon alas, my fat rump!
My fat rump, I have lost you!
Valley after valley, little valleys—
Boy, settle along those little valleys.
May your own kin become your enemies,
May you become just like me!
Your father Manas was a hero,
A lion who shook the world.
Semetey, son of that lion,
To Temir Khan's city
What of you, who came wandering?
My kinsman trampled me, made me a dog;
I could not win equality against that villain.
Temir Khan inflicted humiliation,
And blackened with soot from quenching charcoal,
Master of a great forest,
What of me, quenching charcoal?
When your fierce father died,
And great oppression in Talas
Was suffered by your unfortunate mother,
Abyke and Kobosh became enemies.
The wealth left by your father,
When they divided it, measured by the whip,
You and your mother, tormented wanderers,
Fled and came to Bukhara.
Your crafty mother, a farmer of wisdom,
Said, 'If I deceive him, he will survive.'
His twig was cut off,
His rite was performed.
She agreed to what he said,
And gave you to Ysmayyl.
What of the Kyrgyz people in Talas?
Not knowing your khan father,
What of you, living as a wanderer?
What of the willow planted on the bank?
A prince's son—
What reason has he to live in flight?
What of the willows planted in even rows?
Orphan slave, what reason have you for this recklessness?
Listen, orphan!
Where are the ocean-like Kyrgyz people?
Son of a father who stood an equal,
Just listen, orphan slave:
Is there any cause to wander?
You were the son of Manas, that noble racer,
Yet you wandered to Bukhara and settled.
Before you reached twelve years of age,
To a schemer like your grandfather Temir Khan
You became a slave in bondage.
In this city of Bukhara,
Making her eat a little falcon's flesh,
Is there anyone shameless as you?
Your fierce mother—
You let them call her a wandering woman.
Bukhara's people surge like waves:
This Bukhara will be no homeland for you.
Though you remain ninety years, bonded slave,
These Tajiks will be no people of yours.
Those Kyrgyz are your own community,
Akun Khan is your father-in-law,
Aychurok is your wife.
Your horse has a white blaze,
Your father is someone else.
Khan Manas, the lord, is your father,
Kanykei, living as a fugitive,
That bereaved woman is your mother.
Because of ill-starred kin,
What of me, living as an exile?
Suffering bitter torment, from Talas
What of you, who came wandering?
You raise a tumult halfway along the road,
Beating a poor man like me,
You choke the poor.
Your father Manas was a hero,
A lion who shook the world.
One like your father, the one God
Will never create among mortals,
Bring forth upon the earth,
Or grant to us again.
The reason he will not grant another:
Your father was the support of the faith,
Your father, distinguished Manas,
Stood apart from the whole universe.
